title: What is sales multithreading? A B2B buying-committee example
summary: Learn how sales multithreading works, who to involve, and how to coordinate conversations, with a B2B example and stakeholder worksheet.
body_markdown:
Sales multithreading means building relationships with several people involved in a purchase at the same company. They may approve the budget, review technical requirements, use the product, or help colleagues agree on a decision.


A department head might be interested in your product while someone else controls the spending or reviews the implementation. Multithreading helps you understand who has those responsibilities and bring them into the conversation.[LinkedIn describes the approach](https://www.linkedin.com/business/sales/blog/modern-selling/how-to-multithread-in-sales) as building multiple relationships within one account.


The fictional example below shows how to do this, with a stakeholder worksheet you can adapt for your own accounts.


## Single-threaded, multithreaded, and multichannel sales


Approach What it describes Example


Single-threaded sales Your relationship with an account depends on one person All conversations and updates go through a department head


Multithreaded sales You build relationships with several people involved in the purchase You discuss workflows with users and implementation requirements with IT


Multichannel outreach You use more than one communication channel You contact someone through email, phone, and LinkedIn


Reaching one person through several channels still leaves you dependent on their involvement. Finding several names gives you people to research; you still need to understand their responsibilities and start useful conversations.


## When sales multithreading is useful


Consider multithreading when a purchase involves several departments, separate budget approval, or technical and implementation reviews. It can help you uncover concerns that your first contact does not handle. Having other relationships also reduces your dependence on that person if their role or availability changes.


[Highspot’s framework](https://www.highspot.com/blog/multithreading-in-sales/) stresses the need to understand stakeholder influence and share account context across the selling team.


Keep the work proportionate to the purchase. If one person can evaluate, approve, and use a straightforward product, an elaborate committee map may add little. For a more complex purchase, find out which responsibilities need to be covered before deciding whom to involve.


## Who might be on a B2B buying committee?


A buying committee is the group involved in evaluating and approving an organizational purchase. Common roles include:


Role What to find out


Champion Do they actively support the purchase and help build internal agreement?


Economic or financial buyer Who controls the budget and can approve spending?


Technical evaluator Who reviews integration, security, implementation, or other technical requirements?


End user Who will use the product and assess its effect on daily work?


Procurement or legal reviewer Do purchasing procedures, contracts, or vendor checks require their involvement?


[LinkedIn’s buying-committee resource](https://business.linkedin.com/sell/resources/sales-terms/buying-committee) describes champion, financial-buyer, technical-buyer, and user roles. One person may have several responsibilities, and an account may need additional reviewers.


Confirm who does what for this particular purchase. A senior title alone tells you little about budget authority. Ask how similar purchases have been approved and who needs to participate this time.


## A fictional sales multithreading example


Suppose you sell customer-support software to a B2B software company. Maya, its Head of Support, tells you that ticket handoffs between teams are causing delays. She agrees to explore alternatives and identifies Theo, a team lead, as someone who would use the product.


Your research also finds Arun, an IT Manager, and Elena, a Finance Director. Their titles suggest possible responsibilities, although nobody at the account has confirmed their involvement.


All names and circumstances in this example are fictional.


### Separate evidence from assumptions in your stakeholder map


Person and possible role What you know Concern to investigate Next question or action


Maya: problem owner; possible champion She described the handoff problem and agreed to explore options What improvement would justify a change? Confirm whether she can coordinate an evaluation


Theo: potential user Maya identified him as someone who would use the product How would a new workflow affect the team? Ask Maya whether Theo should help evaluate it


Arun: possible technical evaluator Research found his title; purchasing role unconfirmed Who handles integration and data-access reviews? Ask Maya who owns the technical assessment


Elena: possible budget approver Research found her title; approval authority unconfirmed Which budget would fund the purchase? Confirm the approval process before requesting a finance discussion


In your own worksheet, record where each piece of information came from and when you learned it. Keep track of whether you have confirmed the person’s buying role and whether they have engaged with you.


### Plan the next conversation


Ask Maya how the evaluation would work. For example:


> To assess the handoff problem properly, who else would need to review the workflow? Would it help to include Theo, and who normally checks integrations before your team chooses a tool?


If Maya agrees to introduce Theo and identifies Arun as the technical reviewer, update the map. Maya has confirmed Arun’s role, though you are still waiting for an introduction. Finance approval remains an open question, and you have yet to establish whether the other people support the purchase.


## How to identify and involve the right people


### 1. Start with the problem and account fit


Identify the team experiencing the problem and the functions a change would affect. Your[ideal customer profile](https://blog.floworks.ai/ideal-customer-profile-template/) can help you decide whether the account belongs in your target market.


Research likely roles through company pages, professional profiles, and relevant company announcements. Record what each source tells you. A profile may confirm a job title while leaving the person’s role in this purchase unknown.


### 2. Ask your current contact about the buying process


Check your assumptions during discovery conversations. Useful questions include:


- Who would use or maintain this if you adopted it?
- How did your team approve a similar purchase last time?
- Which reviews would need to happen before you could proceed?
- Who else should help define the evaluation criteria?


Your contact can explain how the organization works and help you avoid reaching out to people who have no responsibility for the purchase.


### 3. Request introductions with a specific reason


Explain what you need to learn from another conversation. In the fictional example, IT could clarify integration requirements. A user could point out workflow problems that the department head does not see every day.


[UserGems recommends](https://www.usergems.com/blog/sales-multithreading) working with your existing contact to identify relevant people and explaining why you want to involve them. You could ask:


> Would you be comfortable introducing the person who reviews integrations? I’d like to understand their requirements before we suggest an evaluation plan. We can keep you included in the conversation.


### 4. Give each person relevant information


Keep the purpose of the evaluation consistent, and address the questions each person is responsible for. Theo could help assess daily ticket handling, while Arun could explain the technical review requirements. Once you confirm who approves the budget, ask what evidence they need to justify spending.


Share the context you have already gathered so each person does not have to repeat the same discovery conversation. Explain the particular question you need their help answering instead of sending everyone an identical message.


### 5. Coordinate follow-up and update the map


Give each relationship a clear owner on your sales team. Record the discussion and unresolved questions, along with the agreed next step. Colleagues can then follow up without sending duplicate or conflicting messages.


Update the map when the buyer adds a reviewer, changes requirements, or moves responsibility to someone else. Keep each status clear. Finding a person, receiving an introduction, speaking with them, and confirming their role in the purchase are different stages.


## Common mistakes to avoid


A contact record can tell you whom to research, but it does not show whether that person has engaged with you or supports the purchase. Confirm their responsibility before treating them as part of the buying committee.


Coordinate additional conversations with your main contact where possible. Explain how each introduction would help the evaluation, and agree on a sensible sequence instead of contacting everyone at once.


When reviewing progress, ask what you have learned and whether the buyer has agreed to a next step. The number of contacts alone cannot answer those questions.

## Frequently asked questions


### How many people should you involve in sales multithreading?


The number depends on the responsibilities involved in the purchase. One person may cover several responsibilities at a smaller account. A more complex purchase may require separate conversations about the budget, technical requirements, user needs, and procurement. Confirm who handles each responsibility.


### What if your main contact resists involving colleagues?


Ask what makes additional involvement difficult and explain the question you need help resolving. Your contact may prefer to gather an answer internally or involve colleagues later. Agree on an alternative and revisit it when appropriate. Resistance alone does not tell you that the contact lacks influence or that the deal will fail.


### How do you know whether multithreading is working?


Look for a clearer understanding of the buying process, participation from relevant people, and agreed next steps. Track unresolved responsibilities and evaluation requirements alongside engagement. More contacts in the CRM give you little evidence of progress unless you are also learning how the decision will happen.
